heading: Before there were area codes
paragraphs: Before you could tap a name on your phone and hear someone's voice, making a call meant turning a dial.

On a rotary phone, you placed your finger in the hole beside a number and pulled the dial around until it stopped. Then you let go. As the dial spun back, it sent a series of electrical pulses down the telephone line. Dial a 3, and it sent three pulses. Dial a 7, and it sent seven. Zero was the exception: it sent ten.
These pulses were how the telephone network understood the number you were calling.

As the telephone system grew, connecting calls between different parts of the country became more complicated. The solution was a national numbering plan. In 1947, AT&T assigned area codes to geographic territories across the United States and Canada.
An area code was the first part of a telephone number. It told the switching equipment where a call needed to go before the rest of the number directed it to a local exchange.
But there was something unusual about the original system: area codes took different amounts of time to dial.
A code like 2-1-2, assigned to New York City, took just five pulses. A code like 6-0-5, assigned to South Dakota, took 21.
That difference is the starting point for this map.

heading: Who got the fast codes
paragraphs: New York City got 2-1-2, five clicks, the fastest code on the plan. Its territory held 7.9 million people in 1950, more than any other. Chicago's 3-1-2 and Los Angeles's 2-1-3 took six clicks; Detroit's 3-1-3 and Pittsburgh's 4-1-2 took seven. The six codes that cost seven clicks or fewer served territories with a median population of 4.3 million. The big industrial cities of 1947 sit at the bright end of the scale.
The plan gave the United States 77 codes and Canada nine. Most of the country took between twelve and twenty clicks to reach, and the 42 codes in that band served a median population of 1.6 million.

At the slow end, South Dakota's 6-0-5, South Carolina's 8-0-3 and North Carolina's 7-0-4 each took 21 clicks, four times New York. South Dakota had 651,000 people. But 7-0-4 covered all of North Carolina, 4.1 million people, so the slow codes went to whole states rather than simply to small populations. The ten codes at 20 or 21 clicks served a median population of 666,000.

The usual explanation is that the busiest places received the shortest codes, saving time on millions of calls. The pattern is there in the data. Whether it was the stated reason is disputed, and this map does not settle it.

heading: A 0 in the middle
paragraphs: The middle digit was a flag. Only area codes had a 0 or 1 there, which let the switching equipment tell an area code from a local exchange. A 0 meant one code for the whole state, like Florida's 3-0-5. A 1 meant the state was split, like the four Texas codes. Of the 77 United States codes, 35 covered whole states.

heading: Running out of numbers
paragraphs: The format allowed 152 codes. The first split came in 1948, when 2-1-9 was cut out of Indiana's 3-1-7. By 1960 the country carried 101 codes, and by 1990 only 114: the plan held for forty years. Then growth used it up. Territories kept splitting, and from 1992 new codes were laid over old ones instead of dividing them; 9-1-7 over Manhattan was the first. The count went from 121 codes in 1992 to 233 in 2000. The last boundary split was 5-7-5 out of New Mexico's 5-0-5 in 2007. Every code since has been an overlay, which is why the hatching appears in the film but the lines stop moving.

In 2025 the lower 48 states carry 367 codes on 237 territories. Eleven territories carry three or more, and Houston's 7-1-3 carries five. The 1947 shape still shows through: 2-1-2 is still Manhattan, 3-1-3 is still Detroit.

heading: How the map was made
paragraphs: Nobody publishes a map of the 1947 area codes. What exists is a map of today's boundaries, a list of the original 77, and a long record of which code was carved out of which. The three were stitched together into one dataset.

Each code has a parent, the code it was split from, and a year. Written down for all 425 codes, that is a family tree with 86 roots. To draw any year, take each of today's territories, follow its parents back until you reach a code that existed that year, and merge the territories that land on the same code. For 1947 the 237 modern territories collapse into the 77 originals.

The modern boundaries came from a 2015 dataset published by UCLA's map library. Where two codes met, each side had its own slightly different copy of the shared edge, so the shapes were snapped together as one surface before anything was drawn. Population per territory is the 1950 Census count of the counties inside it; the 77 territories add up to 150.7 million people, the Census figure for the 48 states. The count of codes in service was checked against the numbering authority's records for twelve years between 1947 and 2025, and all twelve match.
One map engine draws every frame of the film and the poster, so the two never disagree.
